analysis.one_liner: Ends the federal tax deduction for punitive damages paid by companies found liable for wrongdoing.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Finance Committee after being introduced with one cosponsor in May 2022.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, when a court or jury orders a company to pay punitive damages—the penalty money meant to punish serious misconduct—the company can often deduct that payment on its federal taxes, and insurance payouts that cover the penalty don't count as taxable income. This bill would disallow the deduction for punitive damages in any judgment or settlement and make insurance reimbursements for those penalties taxable income, so the punishment would actually cost the wrongdoer money instead of being partially shifted to taxpayers.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers and the federal treasury, since companies that are punished for misconduct could no longer reduce their tax bill by the amount of the penalty, and juries' penalties would remain meaningful rather than being partially reimbursed by taxpayers. It also strengthens deterrence: if wrongdoers must bear the full cost of penalties themselves, they have more reason not to cause harm in the first place.

how_it_helps.text: Denies any tax deduction for punitive damages paid or incurred in connection with a judgment or settlement in any legal action.
Requires that insurance payments, or any other payments made on a taxpayer's behalf, to cover punitive-damages liability be counted as taxable income.
Current law already denies deductions for antitrust treble damages and for payments tied to violating laws, but leaves ordinary punitive damages deductible; this bill closes that gap.

analysis.who_pays: Companies found liable for punitive damages and the insurers that write coverage for such penalties. A company penalized for harming people would pay the full penalty with no tax offset, and a settlement or insurance payout to cover punitive damages would itself trigger tax liability, making that insurance less useful.

drawbacks.text: An honest objection is the general double-tax concern: tax law normally lets businesses deduct ordinary costs of doing business, and defendants argue that removing this deduction punishes the same conduct twice—once by the jury and once at tax time.

Because insurance payments to cover punitive damages would become taxable income, insurers' products covering such liability become less valuable, which could raise the cost or reduce availability of liability insurance for businesses generally, not only wrongdoers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit is real but targeted: it removes a tax break that lets companies treat their own punishments as a deductible business cost, and makes sure the penalty lands on the wrongdoer rather than on taxpayers. The main honest cost is the standard double-recovery argument and possible pressure on liability insurance markets. The bill is narrowly drafted—it touches only punitive damages, not compensatory damages—so it would not disrupt normal tax deductions for legitimate business costs.

outcome.mechanism: Leahy introduced the bill in May 2022 and it was sent to the Senate Finance Committee, where no action was ever taken; the two-year Congress ended with it still parked in committee.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on May 26, 2022, read twice, and referred to the Committee on Finance.
That was the bill's only recorded action; no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever followed before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
The bill had one Democratic cosponsor alongside its sponsor, and no Republican support is recorded.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that pay punitive damages and their insurers are better off, because the tax write-off for penalties remained intact for the entire Congress; no vote ever forced senators to go on record for or against it.

for.name: Patrick Leahy
for.role: U.S. Senator from Vermont (pro Tempore Emeritus)
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate in May 2022.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Sen. Ron Wyden, D-OR)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled, and the bill died in committee when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Only two senators are on record supporting the bill—the sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor—and no senator is recorded as opposing it, so no party split can be measured.

industries.note: Insurers sell coverage that pays punitive damages on behalf of corporate clients; the bill would make those payouts taxable income to the insured, reducing the value of that coverage and making it harder to shift the cost of wrongdoing to others.
Companies facing punitive damages currently deduct the payments from taxable income, cutting the effective cost of a jury penalty by roughly the corporate tax rate; the bill removes that offset.

The bill applies to settlements as well as judgments, which could change how companies and plaintiffs structure settlement negotiations over punitive claims, with both sides facing new tax consequences.
